cards.title: Imine, Molli, Oster and Rusinowitch
cards.sub: 2003 · ECOO and CASSIS teams, LORIA, Nancy
cards.prompt: They pointed a theorem prover at operational transformation, and they were not trying to end it. What were they trying to make cheap, and what did the same paper go on to propose?
cards.answer: The proof. Write the transformation functions in first-order logic and SPIKE checks both correctness conditions in seconds or minutes, instead of a human walking 123 cases and starting over every time a function changes. The paper then proposes its own new set of transformation functions for strings and states it correct with respect to both conditions - the set a later report calls IMOR and demolishes.
cards.body: Two INRIA Lorraine teams at LORIA in Nancy: ECOO, who built groupware, and CASSIS, who did formal verification. Their complaint about operational transformation was cost, not doubt. Proving the second condition on a string is "123 different cases to explore", and the proof dies every time a function definition changes.

cards.title: SPIKE breaks its own authors' functions
cards.prompt: The same prover cleared these functions in 2003 and produced a counterexample against them two years later. The functions had not changed. What had - and why is that the more useful half of the story?
cards.answer: The specification. The 2003 model made an insert's transformed position equal to its original position by precondition, so SPIKE never generated the instances where the two differ - the instances that diverge. Rerun without it and the prover returns a three-site scenario on "bcd" that leaves one replica holding "bxxd" and another "bxd". The proof was sound and about the wrong system: a machine proves what you modelled, not what you shipped.
cards.body: The authors' own functions, listed under IMOR, with a counterexample printed underneath: "Unfortunately, we made a mistake in the specification of transformation functions." Same report, section 4: every other published proposal for strings falls the same way, one counterexample each. Ellis's, Ressel's, Suleiman's, SDT's.

cards.title: "Data Consistency for P2P Collaborative Editing"
cards.prompt: A WOOT insert carries no position at all. Name what it carries instead, and the one property of those values that makes the operation safe to apply in any order.
cards.answer: Neighbours: insert this character between that one and that one, each named by identifier. Figure 1 of the paper writes it ins(a ≺ 1 ≺ b), against the position-based ins(2, '1'). The identifier is a pair - site number and that site's clock - so it is unique and never reused. It addresses an element rather than a slot, so nothing another replica does can move it, which is what makes transformation unnecessary.
cards.body: Oster, Urso, Molli and Imine, CSCW 2006, Banff. A W-character is a five-field record: an identifier, the character, a visible flag, and the identifiers of its previous and next characters. The visible flag is the tombstone - delete clears it and the record stays, because some replica may still anchor an insert to it.

cards.title: Both roads end at the graveyard
cards.sub: December 2005 · RR-5795, section 5 · seven months after WOOT's RR-5580
cards.prompt: Both branches of this chapter end up storing dead characters forever, and the OT branch took the trick from the other one. Given that, what does an OT-versus-CRDT call in a design review actually turn on?
cards.answer: Not tombstones - both branches grow a graveyard once replicas are allowed to diverge offline. It turns on where order comes from. Buy a total order from a central sequencer and the transforms only have to satisfy the weaker condition, so real deletes come back and the server becomes the thing that must not fall over. Refuse the sequencer and order comes from immutable per-character identity, paid for in storage that never shrinks.
cards.body: Section 5 of the report, where the OT branch gives in and names the result Tombstone Transformation Functions: "Our idea is to keep the deleted character b as a tombstone. This is a transposition of the WOOT approach ... in the OT framework." Then the same admission WOOT makes: "the space overhead of tombstones grows indefinitely."
